newsitem.title: KUWAIT: US-Kuwait chem plant $1.2 bln loan oversubscribed.
newsitem.headline: US-Kuwait chem plant $1.2 bln loan oversubscribed.

text.p: A $1.2 billion loan to partly finance a U.S.-Kuwaiti petrochemical complex called Equate was heavily oversubscribed, arranger National Bank of Kuwait (NBK) said on Tuesday.

"The transaction received overwhelming success in international markets and was heavily oversubscribed. As a result, both the underwriting banks and the participating banks had to be substantially cut back," NBK said in a statement.
NBK, Kuwait's largest commercial bank, negotiated the loan.
The loan agreement will be signed on September 15 by about 50 international and Gulf banks and financial institutions.

Bankers said the loan was the largest non-recourse project financing ever arranged in the region outside of the crude and refining sector. It is also the first major loan in the region to incorporate a mix of conventional and Islamic financing.
In January, the U.S.-Kuwaiti joint venture awarded a group of Gulf and American banks a mandate to raise $1.2 billion in long-term financing to build the complex south of Kuwait City.

The venture between America's Union Carbide Corp, Kuwait's Petrochemical Industries Co (PIC) and Kuwait's Bubiyan Petrochemical Co turned down an offer by U.S. Eximbank that would have covered almost all the financing.
Total cost will be about $2 billion. The non-debt portion will be obtained from the joint venture partners' equity participation.
NBK and a number of banks and institutions and an Islamic institution, Kuwait Finance House, underwrote it.

The other underwriters are Chase Manhattan, J.P. Morgan & Co, Citibank, Bahrain-based Gulf International Bank, Gulf Investment Corp, Saudi-based Arab Petroleum Investment Corp and Arab Investment Co, Arab Banking Corp, NBK, Kuwaiti commercial banks Gulf Bank, Commercial Bank, al-Ahli Bank and Burgan Bank.
There are two tranches -- $500 million over 10-1/2 years by Kuwaiti-based institutions and $700 million for 8-1/2 years by regional and international institutions, sources have said.
